\title{Invalid Is Not Failure:\\[2pt]
\large Identification, Estimation, and Leaderboard Fragility When\\
Infrastructure Fails in Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation}
\author{Shilin Chhabra\\
University of Wisconsin--Madison\\
\texttt{chhabra7@wisc.edu}}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Long-running agents often stop without a valid outcome because a provider,
runtime, or evaluation harness failed rather than the agent. Leaderboards score
such runs as failures; papers sometimes drop them. We treat this as an
identification problem. \emph{Theory:} when failures are independent of the
agent, both policies are closed-form functions of three numbers, the success
rate and the mean survival of successful and failed runs; rerunning removes only
the between-task part of the distortion; and two agents swap places at a
critical per-step hazard $q^*\approx\ln(p_A/p_B)/(\bar H_{1,A}-\bar H_{1,B})$,
where $\bar H_1$ is the mean length of successful runs. This one-line law
predicts the exact reversal hazard of 424 of the 429 reversing pairs in three
corpora, with rank correlation 0.98 to 0.99. \emph{Estimation:} weighting
needs only observed quantities, a doubly robust estimator also uses each invalid
run's logged prefix, and a parameter $\gamma$ bounds outcome-dependent failure.
\emph{Measurement:} across 542 public submissions to 11 SWE-bench and
Multi-SWE-bench leaderboards, 89\% contain invalid or unattributable runs, and
on SWE-bench Verified 58 orderings pass a paired significance test yet are not
identified by the published evidence. At the leaderboard-wide provider-failure
rate and the container-crash rate observed in public logs, scoring invalid runs
as failures would reverse 11 and 39 of 741 pairs among 39 frontier models. Treating Gemini 3 Pro's 11 provider failures as
censored raises its estimate by 0.7 to 2.6 points (95\% interval) and improves
its rank in 92\% of task resamples. \emph{Validation:} repeated runs and
cross-model task difficulty imply $\gamma$ between 0.46 and 0.82 in all four
real cases we can test, and a replicate-based estimate that does not assume
independence agrees with weighting to within 0.06 points. We release the census,
code, and a minimum validity record for benchmark reports.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A long-horizon agent run can end for two very different reasons. The agent can
fail the task, or the measurement apparatus can fail the agent: a provider
returns 503 until the retry budget is exhausted, a container crashes, the
evaluation harness never produces a verdict. Only the first is evidence about
the agent. Yet benchmark reports usually collapse both into one success rate
through an unstated policy: invalid runs are either scored as failures or
deleted. Leaderboards typically do the former, by dividing resolved tasks by
all tasks.

Validity problems in agent benchmarks are well documented
\citep{kapoor2024agentsthatmatter,weidinger2025evalscience,zhu2026guardrails},
and a recent audit finds that agent benchmark papers disclose little about their
harness and failure handling \citep{moghadasi2026disclose}. Our question is
narrower and statistical: \emph{what does each handling policy estimate, what
can the data identify, and how large are the consequences on real
leaderboards?}

The answer is structural. Suppose infrastructure failures are entirely
independent of the agent, arriving with a small hazard per agent step. Long runs
are exposed more often, so an outcome-independent failure becomes informative at
the trajectory level whenever horizon and success are associated. This is the
situation on every corpus we examine, and it is sharpest on the current
frontier, where models differ several-fold in how many steps they take.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Identification} (Section~\ref{sec:ident}). A validity rule
separating outcomes from censoring; assumption-free bounds; a three-number
characterisation of the two standard policies; a decomposition of rerunning;
weighting without counterfactual horizons and its limit under hard caps; a
critical-hazard law for pairwise reversals; and sharp rank intervals for
leaderboard entries.
\item \textbf{Estimation} (Section~\ref{sec:est}). A doubly robust estimator
that exploits the partial trajectory of every invalid run, and a sensitivity
analysis for outcome-dependent failure.
\item \textbf{Measurement} (Sections~\ref{sec:data}--\ref{sec:real}). A census of
542 public submissions to 11 leaderboards and 23{,}661 frontier runs on two
SWE-bench splits, showing real invalidity, orderings that are significant but
not identified, and real rank changes with sampling uncertainty; plus hazards
calibrated to failure processes observed in public logs.
\item \textbf{Validation} (Section~\ref{sec:tests}). Tests of the
independent-failure assumption on real data, using repeated runs of the same
task and cross-model task difficulty.
\item \textbf{Practice} (Section~\ref{sec:practice}). A minimum validity record
that makes every estimator in this paper computable from logs (the doubly robust
one also needs the logged trajectory).
\end{itemize}

This paper extends a four-page symposium version\footnote{Presented at the AAAI
2026 Fall Symposium on Trustworthy Agentic Systems (TAS 2026). New here: the
critical-hazard law and rank intervals, the estimation theory of
Section~\ref{sec:est}, the leaderboard census and frontier corpora, all
real-censoring analyses and assumption tests, and the fragility results.} whose
formal core is Section~\ref{sec:ident}.

\section{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

A benchmark initiates runs $i=1,\dots,N$ with fixed semantic outcomes
$Y_i\in\{0,1\}$ and horizons $H_i$, the number of agent decision steps the run
would take. The estimand is the corpus reliability $p=N^{-1}\sum_iY_i$.
Randomness enters only through the validity indicators $C_i$ (1 if $Y_i$ is
observed), drawn by the infrastructure with $\pi_i=\Pr(C_i=1)$. This
design-based view matches the finite corpora we analyse; population statements
would need i.i.d.\ sampling of runs.

\begin{definition}[Validity rule]\label{def:validity}
Fix the benchmark specification, which declares the agent's budgets (steps,
tokens, cost, context window, wall-clock) and environment. An interruption at
step $k$ is an \emph{outcome} (a valid failure) if a fault-free execution with
the same agent actions up to $k$ would also have terminated there: budget or
context exhaustion, repeated malformed output, or damage the agent did to its
own environment. It is \emph{censoring} if the fault-free execution would not
have terminated: provider errors after retries, host preemption, harness defects,
an evaluation harness that produced no verdict, and wall-clock timeouts whose
budget was consumed by infrastructure latency. Interruptions that cannot be
attributed either way are a third, reported category handled by bounds.
\end{definition}

The context window is part of the system under test, so context exhaustion is a
valid failure and $p$ is success within the declared budgets. The rule is
decidable from logs when budgets are declared in agent-controlled units.

Let $T_i$ be the step at which infrastructure would first fail run $i$, with
survival $G(h)=\Pr(T>h)$. Run $i$ is valid iff $T_i>H_i$, so $\pi_i=G(H_i)$
when $T\perp(Y,H)$. A constant hazard $q$ gives $\pi_i=s^{H_i}$ with $s=1-q$.
Each run reveals $V_i=\min(H_i,T_i)$, $C_i$, and its trajectory prefix up to
$V_i$. Write $\pb_1$ and $\pb_0$ for the mean of $\pi_i$ over successful and
failed runs, $\pb=p\pb_1+(1-p)\pb_0$, $m=1-\pb$ for the expected invalid
fraction, and $\rho=\pb_1/\pb_0$ for the \emph{survival ratio}.

\section{Identification}
\label{sec:ident}

\begin{proposition}[Assumption-free bounds]\label{prop:bounds}
With $M$ censored runs and $S$ observed successes, and no assumption about the
censored outcomes, $S/N\le p\le(S+M)/N$. For bounded scores $Y_i\in[a,b]$ the
endpoints are $(\sum_iC_iY_i+aM)/N$ and $(\sum_iC_iY_i+bM)/N$.
\end{proposition}

This is the agent-evaluation instance of a worst-case bound
\citep{manski1990nonparametric}. Its first consequence is that the standard
leaderboard score, $S/N$, is the \emph{lower endpoint of the identified
interval}, not an estimate of reliability.

\begin{proposition}[Three numbers determine both policies]\label{prop:three}
For any observation probabilities $\pi_i$, including outcome-dependent ones,
\[
\E[\hat p_{\rm fail}]=p\,\pb_1\le p,\qquad
\frac{p_{\rm cc}}{1-p_{\rm cc}}=\rho\,\frac{p}{1-p},\qquad
p_{\rm cc}-p=\frac{p(1-p)(\pb_1-\pb_0)}{\pb},
\]
where $\hat p_{\rm fail}=N^{-1}\sum_iC_iY_i$ and
$p_{\rm cc}=\sum_i\pi_iY_i/\sum_i\pi_i$ is the probability limit of the
complete-case rate $S/(N-M)$. The expected identified interval is
$[p\pb_1,\,p\pb_1+m]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\sum_i\pi_iY_i=Np\pb_1$ and $\sum_i\pi_i(1-Y_i)=N(1-p)\pb_0$; $\hat p_{\rm fail}$
is linear in $C$.
\end{proof}

Three consequences follow. \emph{Direction:} invalid-as-failure never overstates
$p$; complete-case reporting overstates it iff $\rho>1$ and understates it iff
$\rho<1$, when both policies err downward. \emph{Conservatism:}
invalid-as-failure is conservative for one agent's level but not for
comparisons, since each agent is discounted by its own $\pb_1$.
\emph{Distribution, not mean:} under a constant hazard,
$\pb_y(s)=\E[s^H\mid Y=y]$ is the probability generating function of the horizon
of outcome $y$, so $\rho$ depends on whole distributions; the mean gap enters
only to first order, $\log\rho=q(\bar H_0-\bar H_1)+O(q^2)$, and first-order
stochastic dominance is sufficient but not necessary for $\rho>1$.

\begin{proposition}[Rerun until valid]\label{prop:rerun}
Group runs into cells $c$ (task $\times$ agent) with within-cell law $F_c$ and
weight $w_c$. If each invalid attempt is replaced by an independent fresh
attempt until one is valid, then
\[
p_{\rm rerun}-p=\sum_cw_c\frac{{\rm Cov}_c(Y,\pi)}{\E_c[\pi]},\qquad
p_{\rm cc}-p=\frac{\sum_cw_c{\rm Cov}_c(Y,\pi)+{\rm Cov}_w(p_c,\E_c[\pi])}{\pb}.
\]
Rerunning removes the between-cell term, keeps a within-cell tilt towards
attempts that happened to be short, is exact for deterministic agents, and costs
$\sum_cw_c/\E_c[\pi]$ attempts per task.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Weighting from observables]\label{prop:km}
If $T\perp(Y,H)$, possibly within strata such as provider, and $G>0$ on the
support of $H$, then
$\hat p_{\rm KM}=\sum_iC_iY_i/\hat G(H_i)\big/\sum_iC_i/\hat G(H_i)$, with
$\hat G$ the Kaplan--Meier estimate from $\{(V_i,1-C_i)\}$, is consistent
\citep{kaplan1958nonparametric,robins2000correcting,satten2001kaplan}. Only
valid runs are weighted, and their horizons are observed; no counterfactual
horizon is needed. A deterministic cap (every run longer than $K$ steps
invalidated) keeps $T\perp(Y,H)$ but makes $G(h)=0$ for $h>K$; the weights then
collapse to the complete case and only Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds} remains
valid.
\end{proposition}

\paragraph{When do rankings break?} Comparisons, not levels, are what
leaderboards report. Let agents $A$ and $B$ have $p_A>p_B$, and let $\mu_{y}$ and
$\sigma^2_{y}$ be the mean and variance of the horizon of runs with outcome $y$.

\begin{proposition}[Critical hazard]\label{prop:critical}
Under a constant per-step hazard $q$, invalid-as-failure ranks $B$ above $A$ iff
$\ln(p_A/p_B)<\ln\pb_{1,B}(q)-\ln\pb_{1,A}(q)$. Since
$\ln\E[s^H]=-q\mu+\tfrac{q^2}{2}(\sigma^2-\mu)+O(q^3)$, the reversal hazard is,
to first order,
\[
q^*_{\rm fail}\approx\frac{\ln(p_A/p_B)}{\mu_{1,A}-\mu_{1,B}}
\quad\text{if }\mu_{1,A}>\mu_{1,B},
\]
and no reversal occurs to first order otherwise. For the complete case the
odds and the survival ratio take the same roles:
$q^*_{\rm cc}\approx\ln(\mathrm{odds}_A/\mathrm{odds}_B)/
[(\mu_{1,A}-\mu_{0,A})-(\mu_{1,B}-\mu_{0,B})]$.
\end{proposition}

A relative gap of $x\%$ is erased by a hazard of about $x\%$ divided by the
difference in mean successful horizon. Agents that are close in score but far
apart in horizon, which describes the current frontier, are therefore fragile
at hazards far below any that practitioners would notice.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp rank intervals]\label{prop:rank}
Let each leaderboard entry $j$ have identified interval $[\ell_j,u_j]$ from
Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds}. The set of ranks entry $j$ can take, over all
values of the missing outcomes, is exactly
$\{1+\#\{k:\ell_k>u_j\},\dots,1+\#\{k\neq j:u_k>\ell_j\}\}$ up to ties, and $A$
is identified to rank above $B$ iff $\ell_A>u_B$.
\end{proposition}

Sharpness holds because each entry's missing outcomes are separate unknowns, so
every entry can sit at either end of its interval at the same time. Proofs of
Propositions~\ref{prop:rerun}--\ref{prop:rank} are in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

\section{Estimation from Partial Trajectories}
\label{sec:est}

\paragraph{Doubly robust estimation.} An invalid agent run is not empty: its
prefix up to the failure is logged. Let $x_{it}$ be features of run $i$'s prefix
before step $t$, and $\mu_t(x)=\Pr(Y=1\mid x_{it}=x,H\ge t)$ an outcome model.
In discrete time, with $dN_i(t)=1$ if run $i$ was invalidated during step $t$,
$\lambda(t)$ the censoring hazard and $G(t)=\prod_{s\le t}(1-\lambda(s))$, the
augmented IPCW estimator \citep{robins1992recovery,tsiatis2006semiparametric} is
\begin{equation}
\hat p_{\rm DR}=\frac1N\sum_i\Big[\frac{C_iY_i}{G(H_i)}
+\sum_{t\le V_i}\big(dN_i(t)-\lambda(t)\big)\frac{\mu_t(x_{it})}{G(t)}\Big].
\label{eq:dr}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Double robustness]\label{prop:dr}
If censoring depends on the past only through the observed prefix (in
particular if $T\perp(Y,H)$), $\hat p_{\rm DR}$ is consistent when either the
censoring model $G$ or the outcome model $\mu$ is correct
\citep{bang2005doubly,tsiatis2006semiparametric}. If $\mu_t(x_{it})=Y_i$ the
bracket equals $Y_i$ exactly for every run.
\end{proposition}

The exactness claim is a telescoping identity
(Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}); we use it as a numerical check of our
implementation. Proposition~\ref{prop:dr} also relaxes independence: the
failure hazard may depend on observed history such as tokens consumed or
elapsed steps, which covers quota-driven rate limits. In that case $\lambda$ and
$G$ in \eqref{eq:dr} become run-specific, $\lambda_i(t)$ and $G_i(t)$, modelled
given the prefix; our experiments use only the marginal Kaplan--Meier version.

\paragraph{Outcome-dependent failure.} No weighting method identifies $p$ if
failure depends on the unobserved outcome. We therefore tilt the success odds of
each invalid run by $\gamma$ relative to its independent-censoring prediction
\citep{scharfstein1999adjusting}:
$\operatorname{logit}\Pr(Y=1\mid\text{invalid at }v)=\operatorname{logit}m(v)+\log\gamma$,
where $m(v)=\Pr(Y=1\mid H\ge v)$ is estimated from completed runs with
Kaplan--Meier weights. $\gamma=1$ is independent censoring; $\gamma\to0$ and
$\gamma\to\infty$ recover the two endpoints of Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds}. A
claim is robust if it holds over a stated range of $\gamma$.

\paragraph{Corpora.} Table~\ref{tab:data} summarises the data. The SWE-agent
corpus \citep{yang2024sweagent,nebius2024trajectories} and $\tau$-bench
\citep{yao2025taubench,agentsuite2026taubench} are as in the symposium version;
for the SWE-agent corpus we now also read the trajectory text to build prefix
features. The \emph{frontier corpus} is the SWE-bench Verified bash-only
leaderboard \citep{swebench2026experiments,openai2024swebenchverified}: 40
models evaluated on the same 500 tasks with the same scaffold
\citep{minisweagent2025}. For every run we take the horizon (API calls), cost,
and resolution from the submission's per-instance file and read the harness
exit status from the public trajectory, fetching only the bytes that contain it
(315\,MB in total, instead of full trajectories of a megabyte or more each). Two submissions had per-instance labels that
contradict their own metadata; we rebuilt one from the evaluation reports
(353/500 resolved against a reported 69.6\%) and excluded the other, whose
public artifact holds only 98 of 500 reports. The \emph{Multilingual frontier
corpus} has the same structure for 14 models on 300 tasks, but its trajectories
are not public, so it records horizons and outcomes without exit statuses; we use
it only for declared-hazard analyses. The \emph{leaderboard census} reads every
submission's evaluation outcome lists at pinned commits of the SWE-bench and
Multi-SWE-bench experiment repositories
\citep{swebench2026experiments,multiswebench2025experiments}. We exclude SWE-bench
Multimodal because its published files imply two different task counts (517 and
510), so its scores are not comparable across submissions.

\paragraph{Horizon.} $H$ counts agent decision steps: AI turns in the SWE-agent
corpus (verified exactly on 20 re-fetched trajectories), assistant turns in
$\tau$-bench, and API calls in the frontier corpus.

\paragraph{Classifying invalidity.} Table~\ref{tab:exit} applies
Definition~\ref{def:validity} to every recorded status. In the census, runs with
no evaluation verdict are \emph{evaluation censoring} (SWE-bench:
\texttt{no\_logs}, \texttt{install\_fail}, \texttt{reset\_failed};
Multi-SWE-bench: incomplete or errored evaluation), and runs whose cause cannot
be read from the published files are \emph{unattributable} (SWE-bench:
\texttt{no\_generation}, \texttt{test\_timeout}; Multi-SWE-bench: empty or error
patches and instances missing from every outcome list). A \emph{strict} reading
treats only evaluation censoring as missing; a \emph{broad} reading treats both
classes as missing. An empty patch may well be the agent's own failure, so the
broad reading is an upper envelope that shows what the published evidence cannot
rule out.

\section{Results under Declared Hazards}
\label{sec:hazard}

We first inject censoring with a declared per-step hazard into completed
corpora. This is a \textbf{sensitivity analysis, not a measured outage rate}:
the identities are exact under the injected mechanism, so agreement between
simulation and theory checks the code, not the model. The empirical content is
the outcome-horizon structure of real trajectories, which fixes how much a given
hazard would distort each policy. The SWE-agent and $\tau$-bench grids were
predeclared in the symposium version; analyses of the frontier corpus are new.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_hazard.pdf}
\caption{Reported reliability against a declared per-step hazard. SWE-agent and
frontier successes survive better, so dropping invalid runs inflates
reliability; on $\tau$-bench the complete-case curve is almost flat. Scoring as
failure falls fastest on the frontier, whose runs are longest. Shaded: 95\%
Monte Carlo band of the Horvitz--Thompson estimator (200 replicates).}
\label{fig:hazard}
\end{figure}

\toprule
corpus & $p$ & $\pb_1$ & $\pb_0$ & $\rho$ & $m$ (\%) & drop & fail \\
\midrule
SWE-agent & 16.73 & .864 & .777 & 1.113 & 20.9 & $+1.54$ & $-2.27$ \\
$\tau$-bench & 55.03 & .877 & .869 & 1.009 & 12.6 & $+0.23$ & $-6.75$ \\

$<10^{-15}$).}
\label{tab:three}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Three numbers explain the dissociation.} On SWE-agent the survival
ratio is well above one, so dropping inflates and scoring-as-failure deflates
reliability, a 6.8-point spread at $q=2\%$ (Figure~\ref{fig:hazard},
Table~\ref{tab:three}). On $\tau$-bench $\rho\approx1$, so dropping is nearly
safe while scoring-as-failure costs 12.6 points at $q=2\%$. On the frontier,
horizons are long (successes average 38 steps, failures 51), so a 1\% hazard
invalidates 12--57\% of a model's runs and scoring-as-failure costs up to 38.4
points (DeepSeek V3.2 (high), whose successful runs average 83 steps).

\paragraph{The mean gap is not enough, and both policies can err downward.}
The first-order approximation $\log\rho\approx q(\bar H_0-\bar H_1)$ overstates
SWE-agent's $\log\rho$ by 26\% at $q=1\%$ and 48\% at $q=2\%$. Neither older
corpus satisfies stochastic dominance (Figure~\ref{fig:horizons}), yet $\rho>1$
at every $q\le5\%$. At model level, 5 of 29 $\tau$-bench models and 1 of 39
frontier models (Devstral (2512)) have $\rho<1$; for these, dropping invalid runs also
understates reliability.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_plane_fragility.pdf}
\caption{(a) Every model in the survival plane at $q=1\%$; above the diagonal,
dropping invalid runs overstates reliability. Frontier models spread far along
both axes because their horizons differ several-fold. (b) Share of model pairs
whose order reverses under a declared hazard.}
\label{fig:fragility}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Frontier rankings are fragile.} Because frontier models are close in
score (median gap between adjacent models 1.0 point) and far apart in horizon,
their order is much more sensitive than that of older corpora
(Figure~\ref{fig:fragility}b). Under invalid-as-failure, the first reversal among
the 39 models occurs at a per-step hazard of only 0.0077\%, and two pairs reverse
below 0.01\%; at $q=0.1\%$, which invalidates 4.1\% of
runs on average, 24 of 741 pairs reverse; at $q=0.25\%$ (9.8\% invalid), 69; at
$q=1\%$, 192. Dropping invalid runs is gentler but not safe: 1, 6, and 24 pairs.
On $\tau$-bench the first reversal needs $q=0.32\%$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_critical.pdf}
\caption{(a) The first-order law of Proposition~\ref{prop:critical} against the
exact reversal hazard under invalid-as-failure, for the 424 pairs in three
corpora that reverse by $q=5\%$ and that the law predicts to reverse (it misses
5 of 429); the dotted line is equality. (b) Share of
adjacent leaderboard pairs reversed as the hazard grows, with the constant-hazard
equivalents of the provider-failure rate observed across the bash-only
leaderboard and the container-crash rate observed in the SWE-agent corpus.}
\label{fig:critical}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{A one-line law predicts reversals.} Proposition~\ref{prop:critical}
reduces fragility to two numbers per pair. On the Verified frontier corpus, 361
of 739 pairs reverse by $q=5\%$. For the 356 of these that the first-order law
predicts to reverse, it ranks the exact reversal hazards with Spearman
correlation 0.992 and falls within a factor of two of the exact value for 98.9\%
(median error 3.7\%); the second-order version is within a factor of two for
every pair it predicts (median error 0.5\%). The law
is equally accurate on the Multilingual frontier corpus (91 pairs, correlation
0.976) and on $\tau$-bench (401 pairs, 0.990), see Figure~\ref{fig:critical}a.
It also explains which pairs can reverse at all: invalid-as-failure can only
demote the agent whose successful runs are longer, so 14 of the 36 adjacent
frontier pairs are reversible, and 8 of the 36 reverse at $q\le0.1\%$.

\paragraph{Calibrated to observed failure processes.} To remove the hypothetical
hazard, we estimate step-wise hazards from the invalidations actually recorded in
the logs and expose every model to them. At the provider-failure process pooled
over the bash-only leaderboard (1.5\% of runs invalid on average), scoring
invalid runs as failures would reverse 11 of 741 frontier pairs and move one
model by 2.3 points; at the SWE-agent container-crash process (6.1\% invalid),
39 pairs and 7.8 points; at the process one submission actually experienced on a
bad day (Qwen2.5-Coder 32B Instruct, 36\% invalid), 241 pairs. The Multilingual
frontier corpus behaves the same way (1 and 11 of 91 pairs), while no
$\tau$-bench pair reverses under the two typical processes, because its
horizons are short and nearly outcome-independent.

\paragraph{Rerunning removes most, not all, of the bias.} On SWE-agent's 4{,}219
task$\times$model cells, rerunning until valid removes 70--72\% of the
complete-case bias at every hazard, leaving $+0.44$ points at $q=1\%$ at a cost
of 1.28 attempts per task (Proposition~\ref{prop:rerun}).

\paragraph{Cost, an unbounded metric.} Dropping invalid runs understates the
mean cost per task by 5--76\% across frontier models at $q=1\%$, because the
dropped runs are the long, expensive ones. No assumption-free bound exists for
cost; reports need an explicit model.

\section{Real Invalidity on Public Leaderboards}
\label{sec:real}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_census.pdf}
\caption{(a) Identified intervals for the top 40 of 135 SWE-bench Verified
submissions. Dots are leaderboard scores (resolved over tasks), which are the
lower endpoints; bars extend over evaluation-censored runs (strict) and
additionally over unattributable runs (broad). (b) Share of adjacent leaderboard
orderings the published evidence identifies, for all 11 splits.}
\label{fig:census}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Census.} Across 542 submissions to 11 leaderboards, 481 (89\%)
contain runs that are evaluation-censored or unattributable
(Figure~\ref{fig:census}). On SWE-bench Verified, 35\% of submissions contain
evaluation-censored runs (up to 18\% of a submission) and 70\% contain
unattributable runs (median 0.4\%, up to 24.2\%); 15 have more than 5\% of their
runs in the two classes combined. Leaderboard gaps are small: the median gap
between adjacent Verified submissions is 0.4 points, two tasks. The data
therefore identify 89 of 105 adjacent Verified orderings under the strict reading
and 43 under the broad reading (Lite: 55 and 21 of 66; Test: 18 and 11 of 22).
By Proposition~\ref{prop:rank}, the median Verified submission's rank interval
spans 1 place (strict) or 5 places (broad), and the widest spans 51. On
Multi-SWE-bench, evaluation censoring is rare, so every adjacent ordering is
identified under the strict reading, but empty or error patches are frequent
(up to 95\% of a submission) and the published files do not say whether the
agent or the harness produced them; under the broad reading only 18 of 176
adjacent orderings are identified. The evidence needed to tell these cases apart
is simply not recorded.

\paragraph{Significant but not identified.} Leaderboard comparisons are often
backed by paired significance tests over tasks. For every pair of submissions
with published per-task results we ran a paired $z$-test and cross-tabulated it
with identification. On SWE-bench Verified, 8{,}001 of 9{,}008 pairs differ
significantly at the 5\% level, yet 58 of them are not identified even under the
strict reading, and 163 under the broad reading (Lite: 31 and 212; Test: 12 and
29). Across all 11 splits, 101 significant orderings are not identified under the
strict reading and 2{,}506 under the broad reading. A significance test that
treats invalid runs as failures certifies orderings the data do not support.

\paragraph{Frontier provider failures.} Seven of 39 frontier submissions lost
runs to provider errors after the harness's retries, 305 runs in all, of which
304 are scored as unresolved (Table~\ref{tab:frontier}). Qwen2.5-Coder 32B
Instruct lost 278 of 500 runs (56\%): its leaderboard score of 9.0\% sits at the
bottom of an identified interval of $[8.8,64.4]\%$ (the lower endpoint is below
the score because one provider-failed run is marked resolved). Complete-case reporting would give 19.8\%, but the failures
struck long runs, which rarely succeed, so Kaplan--Meier weighting with the
observed failure step gives 10.3\%, and the sensitivity analysis gives
9.2--13.9\% for $\gamma\in[1/4,4]$. The rank is unchanged either way. Gemini 3
Pro lost only 11 runs (2.2\%), but it sits in the densest part of the
leaderboard: weighting moves it from 12th (tied; 14th at its officially reported
score) to 9th, and it ranks 9th or 10th for every $\gamma\in[1/4,4]$, that is,
even if its failed runs were four times less likely to succeed than comparable
completed runs. Task sampling adds its own uncertainty, which we quantify with
a paired bootstrap that resamples the 500 tasks jointly for all 39 submissions
(2{,}000 resamples). The correction itself is robust: the weighted estimate
exceeds the leaderboard score by 0.7 to 2.6 points (95\% interval) and improves
the rank in 92\% of resamples. The absolute rank is not: its 95\% interval runs
from 7th to 16th on the leaderboard score and from 5th to 14th after weighting.
For Qwen2.5-Coder the correction is 0.4 to 2.2 points, with no rank change.

\paragraph{Container failures in the SWE-agent corpus.} The corpus's
\texttt{early\_exit} status is set only when the container runtime raises during
a step \citep{sweagent2024code}. It marks 3{,}176 runs (4.0\%), none resolved.
The identified interval is $[16.73,20.70]\%$; complete-case gives 17.42\%;
model-stratified Kaplan--Meier gives 17.09\%; the doubly robust estimator, which
also uses each crashed run's logged prefix, gives 17.10\%; and $\gamma\in[1/4,4]$ gives 16.8--17.8\%. The corpus label is the lower
endpoint.

\section{Testing the Independence Assumption on Real Data}
\label{sec:tests}

Weighting assumes that an invalidated run would have succeeded as often as a
completed run that reached the same step ($\gamma=1$). Two structures in public
data let us test this without running any agent.

\paragraph{Repeated runs of the same task.} In the SWE-agent corpus,
task$\times$model cells hold many runs (median 13); we use the 3{,}157 crashed
runs whose cell has at least three completed runs. Container crashes are
\emph{not} independent of the task: they occur in 5.0\% of runs in cells that
never succeed and in 1.6\% of runs in cells that succeed at least 60\% of the
time. Weighting, however, conditions on the failure step, and hard tasks are
also the long ones. The completed runs in a crashed run's own cell imply that
crashed runs would have succeeded 7.8\% of the time; the step-based imputation
used by weighting says 9.4\%. The implied $\gamma$ is 0.82, and the reliability
estimate built from cell-mates, which does not assume independence, is 17.04\%,
against 17.10\% from weighting, 17.42\% from dropping, and 16.73\% from the
corpus label.

\paragraph{Cross-model task difficulty.} On the frontier leaderboard, the other
38 models' results measure how hard each task is. Qwen2.5-Coder's provider
failures struck slightly harder tasks (mean cross-model success 0.59 against
0.65). Conditioning on both the failure step and task difficulty, its failed runs
would have succeeded 2.1\% of the time, against 2.6\% under the step-based
imputation ($\gamma=0.78$), for an estimate of 9.9\% against 10.3\% from
weighting. A difficulty-only imputation would claim 17.3\%, because it ignores
that these runs were still running at step 52 on average while Qwen's successful
runs average 16 steps; the failure step carries most of the information. For
gpt-oss-120b the implied $\gamma$ is 0.80 (26.2\% against 26.3\%). Gemini 3 Pro's
11 failures struck much harder tasks (0.47 against 0.61), giving $\gamma=0.46$
and an estimate of 71.8\% against 72.2\%, still above its leaderboard score.

\paragraph{What the tests show.} In all four cases the implied $\gamma$ lies
between 0.46 and 0.82, inside the range $[1/4,4]$ we use for sensitivity
analysis, and the resulting estimates move by at most 0.4 points. Infrastructure
failures in these logs lean slightly towards harder tasks than their failure
step alone suggests, so weighting estimates are, if anything, slightly
optimistic. They are closer to the replicate- and difficulty-based estimates
than invalid-as-failure in all four cases, and closer than dropping in three
(for Gemini 3 Pro the two coincide).

\section{Estimators in Practice}
\label{sec:estimators}

\paragraph{Weighting from observables.} Simulating failure times step by step
and estimating $G$ only from $(V_i,C_i)$, Kaplan--Meier weighting has bias at
most 0.015 points on SWE-agent and 0.008 on $\tau$-bench under constant hazards
up to 2\%, and at most 0.024 under a hazard that doubles after step 25, where a
constant-hazard fit is biased by $+0.33$ to $+0.67$ points. Estimated weights are
more efficient than true ones (standard deviation 0.25 against 0.37 points on
$\tau$-bench at $q=1\%$), as theory predicts \citep{robins1994estimation}.
Under a hard cap at 25 steps on SWE-agent, weighting collapses to the complete
case (23.04\% against a true 16.73\%) and only the bounds
$[15.05,49.73]\%$ remain valid.

\paragraph{Doubly robust estimation.} We fit $\mu$ on completed runs with
weights $\hat G(t-1)/\hat G(H_i)$ and two-fold cross-fitting by task, using 22
prefix features: elapsed steps; counts of edit, create, run, navigation, test,
and reproduction actions; failed edits; observation errors and apparent test
passes; whether a clean run or a passing observation followed the last edit;
steps since the last edit; and the model. We compare two outcome models, a
logistic regression and a gradient-boosted classifier. The implementation
satisfies the exactness identity of Proposition~\ref{prop:dr} to machine
precision. Prefixes are informative but far from decisive: the out-of-fold AUC
for eventual success rises from 0.48 at step~1 to 0.72 (logistic) and 0.75
(boosted) at step~40 (Figure~\ref{fig:dr}b). Figure~\ref{fig:dr}a shows the three
properties the theory predicts (30 replicates per scenario).
\emph{Robustness to the censoring model:} under the step-dependent hazard,
constant-hazard weighting is biased by $+0.67$ points, and adding the prefix
model cuts the bias to $-0.04$ (logistic) or $-0.05$ (boosted).
\emph{Robustness to the outcome model:} with correct Kaplan--Meier weights, a
deliberately wrong constant $\mu=0.5$ leaves the estimator unbiased ($+0.01$,
first iteration with 50 replicates). \emph{Efficiency:} at $q=2\%$ the boosted
prefix model lowers the standard deviation from 0.097 to 0.083 points relative to
Kaplan--Meier weighting and from 0.186 to 0.081 relative to constant-hazard
weighting, with bias below 0.01 points. On the real container failures the
doubly robust and weighted estimates agree (17.10\%), which is consistent with
those failures being unrelated to the modelled prefix features once the failure
step is known. The prefix thus buys insurance against a wrong censoring model
and an efficiency gain that grows with the quality of the outcome model.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_dr.pdf}

\section{A Minimum Validity Record}
\label{sec:practice}

Every estimator in this paper except the doubly robust one, which also needs
the logged trajectory, is computable from five fields per run:
(1) the task and agent; (2) the termination reason, classified by
Definition~\ref{def:validity}; (3) the step (and, if relevant, tokens and
wall-clock) at termination; (4) the outcome, if one was produced; and (5) the
number of attempts, if reruns were used. A report should then give the
initiated and valid run counts, invalid counts by class, the policy applied,
and the interval of Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds} next to the headline number.
None of the public artifacts we examined records all five fields in one place;
the frontier corpus comes closest, since its trajectories carry both exit status
and step count.

\section{Related Work}

\citet{zhao2026failure} anatomise coding-agent failure over complete
trajectories. \citet{ruan2026doomed} abort episodes predicted to fail; this
removes outcomes deliberately as a function of predicted failure, which is
outcome-dependent censoring outside our independent-failure model.
\citet{li2026early} study failure-aware observability but do not pose
infrastructure termination as a missing-outcome problem;
\citet{gonuguntla2026replay} shows static replay under a substituted model scores
a counterfactual world. \citet{wang2026interface} uses ``censoring'' for
interface-level output suppression, and \citet{raghu2026proper} extend proper
scoring rules to administratively censored trajectories, the closest work,
though it scores predictions rather than identifying an aggregate estimand.
Disclosure and validity work
\citep{kapoor2024agentsthatmatter,weidinger2025evalscience,zhu2026guardrails,chen2026judge,moghadasi2026disclose}
reports what happened; we study how missing outcomes change the estimand and
what the published evidence identifies. Our estimators are classical
\citep{horvitz1952generalization,kaplan1958nonparametric,manski1990nonparametric,robins1992recovery,robins1994estimation,bang2005doubly,scharfstein1999adjusting};
the contribution is their mapping onto agent evaluation, the three-number,
rerun, and critical-hazard results, sharp rank intervals for leaderboards, the
use of partial trajectories, tests of the assumptions on real data, and
measurement on public leaderboards.

\section{Limitations}

(1) The declared-hazard results are a sensitivity analysis, now anchored by
hazards estimated from real logs; the real-censoring results rest on exit
statuses whose attribution we classify by Definition~\ref{def:validity}, and some
statuses are unattributable. (2) Weighting assumes failure independent of the
outcome given the failure step; the tests of Section~\ref{sec:tests} cover four
real cases, and the $\gamma$ analysis bounds departures without removing them.
(3) The census reads published outcome lists; an empty patch or a missing
generation may be the agent's own failure, which is why we report strict and
broad readings, and a few Multi-SWE-bench submissions report different task
totals for the same language. (4) The frontier corpora use one scaffold, and two
submissions required label repair or exclusion. (5) Sampling uncertainty over
tasks is quantified for the real rank changes and in the significance
cross-tabulation, but not for every declared-hazard result. (6) We did not run a
live fault-injection study. With deterministic inference, a run invalidated at
step $t$ is exactly its fault-free run truncated at $t$, so injecting censoring
into completed trajectories already gives ground truth for the censoring
mechanism; what a live study would add is realism of the failure process, which
Section~\ref{sec:hazard} instead calibrates to failure processes observed in
public logs.

\section{Conclusion}

An invalid execution is not a failed one. On public leaderboards, runs lost to
providers, containers, and evaluation harnesses are scored as failures, which
reports the lower end of what the data identify; dropping them tilts the odds;
rerunning fixes only part. A one-line law says when rankings break: when the
relative gap between two agents falls below the hazard times the difference in
their successful horizons. Because frontier models are close in score and far
apart in horizon, that happens at failure rates already present in public logs,
and significance tests that ignore invalid runs certify orderings the evidence
does not support. The remedy is cheap: record each run's termination reason and
step, report identified intervals and rank intervals, and estimate with weights,
and with the partial trajectory, when independence is defensible; on the four
real cases we could test, departures from it were small.

\appendix

\section{Proofs}
\label{app:proofs}

\paragraph{Proposition~\ref{prop:rerun}.} Attempts in cell $c$ are i.i.d.\ from
$F_c$, each valid with probability $G(H)$ independently, so the first valid
attempt has density $G(h)\,dF_c(y,h)/\E_c[G(H)]$ and success probability
$\E_c[Y\pi]/\E_c[\pi]=p_c+{\rm Cov}_c(Y,\pi)/\E_c[\pi]$. Averaging with weights
$w_c$ gives the first identity; the law of total covariance applied to
$p_{\rm cc}=\sum_cw_c\E_c[Y\pi]/\pb$ gives the second. The number of attempts is
geometric with mean $1/\E_c[\pi]$.

\paragraph{Proposition~\ref{prop:km}.} Under $T\perp(Y,H)$ the observed pairs
$(V_i,1-C_i)$ are a right-censored sample of $T$ with independent censoring by
$H$, so $\hat G$ is consistent for $G$ wherever the risk set is non-empty
\citep{kaplan1958nonparametric}. Since $\E[C_i\mid Y_i,H_i]=G(H_i)$, the
weighted numerator and denominator are consistent for $Np$ and $N$
\citep{satten2001kaplan}. Under a cap, every run with $H>K$ is invalidated at
$K+1$, so $\hat G(K+1)=0$ and valid runs all have weight $\hat G(H_i)^{-1}=1$.

\paragraph{Proposition~\ref{prop:critical}.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:three},
$\E\hat p_{{\rm fail},A}<\E\hat p_{{\rm fail},B}$ iff
$\ln p_A+\ln\pb_{1,A}(q)<\ln p_B+\ln\pb_{1,B}(q)$. With $s=1-q$,
$\pb_1(q)=\E[e^{H\ln s}\mid Y=1]$ is the moment generating function of the
success horizon at $\ln s=-q-q^2/2+O(q^3)$, so its logarithm, the cumulant
generating function, is $\ln s\,\mu_1+(\ln s)^2\sigma_1^2/2+O(q^3)
=-q\mu_1+\tfrac{q^2}{2}(\sigma_1^2-\mu_1)+O(q^3)$. Substituting and keeping the
linear term gives the stated root; keeping the quadratic term gives the
second-order version used in Section~\ref{sec:hazard}. The complete case follows
in the same way from the odds identity of Proposition~\ref{prop:three}, with
$\ln\rho=\ln\pb_1-\ln\pb_0$.

\paragraph{Proposition~\ref{prop:rank}.} Entry $j$'s score can be any value in
$[\ell_j,u_j]$ attainable by its own missing outcomes, independently of every
other entry, because different entries' runs are different unknowns. Entry $j$
is ranked best when it takes $u_j$ and every other entry $k$ takes $\ell_k$,
which leaves exactly the entries with $\ell_k>u_j$ ahead of it; it is ranked
worst when it takes $\ell_j$ and every other entry takes $u_k$, which puts every
entry with $u_k>\ell_j$ ahead. Moving the other entries between their endpoints
one at a time changes $j$'s rank by at most one per move, so, up to ties among
equal scores, every intermediate rank is attained. The ordering of $A$ and $B$
is identified iff it holds at the least favourable values, $\ell_A$ and $u_B$.

\paragraph{Exactness in Proposition~\ref{prop:dr}.} Using
$1/G(t)-1/G(t-1)=\lambda(t)/G(t)$, a run invalidated at step $t_0$ contributes
$\sum_{t<t_0}(-\lambda(t))/G(t)+(1-\lambda(t_0))/G(t_0)=
(1-1/G(t_0-1))+1/G(t_0-1)=1$, and a completed run contributes
$1/G(H)+\sum_{t\le H}(-\lambda(t))/G(t)=1/G(H)+1-1/G(H)=1$. With
$\mu_t(x_{it})=Y_i$ each bracket therefore equals $Y_i$. Double robustness
follows from the standard argument \citep{tsiatis2006semiparametric}: the
augmentation has mean zero when $G$ is correct, and when $\mu$ is correct the
estimating function has mean zero for any $G$ \citep{bang2005doubly}.

\paragraph{Predeclared grids (symposium version).} SWE-agent, true $p=16.73\%$:
at $q=0.1/0.25/0.5/1/2\%$, $p_{\rm cc}=16.91/17.17/17.57/18.27/19.42$ and
$\E\hat p_{\rm fail}=16.48/16.11/15.53/14.46/12.60$. $\tau$-bench, true
$p=55.03\%$: $p_{\rm cc}=55.06/55.09/55.15/55.26/55.43$ and
$\E\hat p_{\rm fail}=54.31/53.26/51.54/48.28/42.39$. Horvitz--Thompson bias never
exceeds 0.005 (SWE-agent) or 0.017 points ($\tau$-bench).

\paragraph{First-iteration doubly robust results.} A first version used a
logistic outcome model with 16 prefix features and 50 replicates in three
scenarios (constant $q=1\%$ and $2\%$, step-dependent $q_0=1\%$). Its results
agree with the main text: under the step-dependent hazard, constant-hazard
weighting was biased by $+0.68$ points and the doubly robust estimator by
$-0.03$; with correct Kaplan--Meier weights, a constant $\mu=0.5$ gave biases of
$+0.010$, $-0.004$, and $+0.012$ points in the three scenarios.

\paragraph{Label repair and exclusion.} The bash-only submission for Gemini 3 Pro
(submitted 2026-02-26 at high reasoning effort) lists every run as unresolved in its per-instance file while its metadata
reports 69.6\%; its 500 public evaluation reports give 353 resolved (70.6\%),
which we use. The submission for Claude 3.7 Sonnet (20250219), run with
mini-SWE-agent v0.0.0,
reports 52.8\% in metadata and 10.2\% in its per-instance file, and only 98 of
500 evaluation reports are public, so we exclude it.

\paragraph{Reproduction.} All inputs are public and no paid API is used.
Code, derived census tables, and the interval tool are released at
\url{https://github.com/chhabrashilin/invalid-is-not-failure}
(Zenodo DOI and Hugging Face dataset/Space URLs: replace this sentence after
minting; keep the GitHub URL if the repository name changes).
\texttt{scripts/censoring/reproduce\_all.py} regenerates the symposium results;
the scripts in \texttt{scripts/extended/} then run in this order:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{fetch\_swebench\_census.py}, \texttt{fetch\_multi\_swe\_bench.py};
\item \texttt{fetch\_bash\_only\_exits.py} (with \texttt{--split verified} and
\texttt{--split multilingual});
\item \texttt{repair\_labels.py}, \texttt{build\_prefix\_features.py};
\item \texttt{census\_leaderboard.py}, \texttt{frontier\_analysis.py},
\texttt{critical\_hazard.py}, \texttt{trace\_driven.py};
\item \texttt{sensitivity.py}, \texttt{assumption\_tests.py},
\texttt{real\_case\_uncertainty.py};
\item \texttt{dr\_estimator.py}, \texttt{dr\_estimator\_v2.py} (needs
scikit-learn);
\item \texttt{make\_extended\_figures.py}.
\end{itemize}
The Gradio app under \texttt{spaces/identified\_intervals/} computes identified
intervals and sharp rank intervals from pasted leaderboard counts.
